newsitem.title: USA: Thousands flock to hear words of Chairman Buffett.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flock to hear words of Chairman Buffett.

text.p: It was a capitalist version of Woodstock.
Some 7,500 shareholders packed an Omaha arena Monday for the Berkshire Hathaway Inc. annual shareholders meeting. Most came to bask in the presence of Warren Buffett, the world's second richest man.

Buffett, Berkshire's chairman, has a personal net worth that Forbes magazine last year estimated at $15.3 billion, second only to Microsoft Corp. co-founder -- and Buffett buddy -- Bill Gates, who was worth $18 billion.

Buffett made his appearance at the cavernous Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum (it's Nebraska spelled backwards), dispatching with the actual business meeting in less than 10 minutes. The main item on the agenda was the re-election of the six-member board of directors, three of whom are named Buffett.
"All in favor say 'Aye,'" Buffett said. "All opposed say 'I'm leaving now.'"

Early arrivals were treated to an hourlong movie titled "Citizen Buffett: Lifestyles of the World's Second Richest Man," a pastiche of old Hollywood film clips, soap opera spoofs, vintage Coca-Cola commercials, footage of Buffett and Gates in China, and a performance by Buffett on the ukulele.
Out in the lobby, vendors hawked an array of products from the Berkshire family -- See's candy, World Book encyclopedias, Dexter shoes, Kirby vacuum cleaners.

Warren Buffett's grown daughter Susie staffed a booth taking orders for Berkshire Hathaway "Activewear" -- T-shirts, golf shirts and sweatshirts emblazoned with a clenched fist holding a wad of dollar bills. "My mother's secretary did the design years ago as a joke," Susie Buffett said. "People kept saying we should sell them, so we did."

Warren Buffett stopped by the booth to pose for photos with his daughter. Seven-year-old Michael Klurfeld from New York City, sporting a baseball cap worn backwards, asked him if Berkshire shares were a superior place to save for college. "Sure," said Susie Buffett, and her father nodded his assent.
Inside the hall, Buffett took questions from the audience for more than five hours, with a 30-minute break for lunch.

The Berkshire shareholders came from all 50 states and most corners of the globe. They peppered the so-called Oracle of Omaha with questions on his investment strategy (he only invests in companies he understands and thinks will be in good shape 10 years from now), techniques for evaluating companies (it's complicated), views of the market (he doesn't make forecasts), investment advice (he doesn't give any, except that he thinks buying Berkshire shares is generally a good idea), opinion on futures and options (he thinks you're better off buying shares) and preferred level for the capital gains tax (he thinks the current 28 percent is about right).
